cur:catacombs2-ravenna-exuperantius-sarc.summary: Between two spiral columns and two palm trees heavy with dates, Christ stands at the centre blessing, flanked by Paul with a book on the left and Peter shouldering the cross on the right. The three figures, set against an empty ground, raise their hands in the gestures of speech and acclamation. An inscription runs along the base below them.
facts: Italian Wikipedia dates it to the second decade of the 5th century; it holds the remains of the Ravenna bishop Exuperantius and, since 1809, those of Archbishop Maximian.
The short sides bear a cross and the monogram of Christ, which appears again on the back between two peacocks and two cypresses.
The sarcophagus now serves as the altar table of a chapel set up in 1701.
cur:catacombs2-ravenna-exuperantius-sarc.notes: The inscription on the base is not transcribed here.

cur:manuscripts-athelstan-psalter-ascens.summary: Headed 'Ascensio Domini', the page shows Christ seated in a mandorla, holding a book and blessing, borne upward between two great angels; below, two more angels address the Virgin, labelled 'Maria', who stands at the centre among the apostles, with the words 'Viri Galilaei' — the angels' question 'Men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven?'.
facts: The Athelstan Psalter is a 9th-century Carolingian psalter to which full-page miniatures were added in England in the 10th century; it is traditionally associated with King Æthelstan, and one of its leaves is now in the Bodleian Library, Oxford (MS Rawl. B 484).
The inscription 'Viri Galilaei' quotes the angels' words to the apostles in the Acts of the Apostles.

cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-insert.summary: On a fragment of a leaf now mounted on a modern support, Christ, haloed and holding a book, sits on a green globe between two angels and holds out a pair of scales, while a crowd of the risen presses toward him from the left. It is a compact image of the Last Judgement within the psalter.
facts: The Stuttgart Psalter was made around 820–830 at the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés near Paris; its 168 leaves contain the psalms with 316 coloured miniatures set between the verses they illustrate.
Its pictures interpret the psalms literally, historically or — very often — Christologically, as prophecies of the life of Christ.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-insert.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature. The leaf is a fragment without a folio number in the WLB foliation; the psalm it accompanied is not legible in the image.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-97-christ.summary: Seated on a globe in the heavens, the beardless Christ-Logos hands a palm to a second figure of himself, cross-nimbed and holding scales, who represents 'his salvation' made known to the nations. Angels approach from both sides, men blow trumpets and the floods clap their hands. The doubling of the figure of Christ is a remarkable theological idea in a drawing.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
The psalter was made in or near Reims, probably under Archbishop Ebbo (816–835); some scholars argue for a date around 850 under his successor Hincmar.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-97-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server. This folio carries two drawings; the crop shows the one for this text.

cur:monumental-coptic-museum-head-of-chr.summary: A frontal bust of Christ with large dark eyes, black hair and beard, and a jewelled cross-nimbus fills a circular medallion, flanked by two winged angels in flight who support it; Greek inscriptions above name the angels and Christ as SOTER, 'Saviour'. The bold outlines and saturated colours are characteristic of Coptic monastic painting.
facts: The painting was discovered in 1976; its provenance is given as the monastery of Apa Apollo at Bawit by most sources, and as Deir el-Muharraq by the Getty database (according to the photographer's notes).
Angels lifting a medallion portrait derive from Roman imagery of victories carrying an imago clipeata, here transferred to Christ.
cur:monumental-coptic-museum-head-of-chr.notes: Provenance uncertain between Bawit and Deir el-Muharraq.

cur:objects-basilewsky-situla.summary: This ivory holy-water bucket is carved in two rows with twelve scenes of Christ's Passion and Resurrection, from the Washing of the Feet and the Betrayal through the Crucifixion to the Harrowing of Hell, Christ's appearances to the women and the apostles, and the Incredulity of Thomas. Small, expressive figures move beneath arcades, while bands of inscription run around the rim. Holy water sprinkled from it over the faithful would have been linked visually to Christ's saving death and rising.
facts: The V&A believes it was made around 980 for the visit of Emperor Otto II, with Theophanu and the infant Otto III, to Milan; only three Ottonian ivory situlae survive (Milan c. 979, this one, and Aachen c. 1000).
Two of its three inscribed bands quote the Carmen Paschale of Sedulius, a 5th-century verse retelling of the Bible.
It passed through the Spitzer and Basilewsky collections and belonged to Tsar Alexander III and the Hermitage before coming to the V&A in 1933.
